paragraphs.heading: What counts as precipitation
paragraphs.text: Precipitation is water that condensed from vapour in the air and then falls from clouds, pulled down by gravity. It comes as drizzle, rain, rain mixed with snow, snow, ice pellets, graupel and hail. It falls once cloud particles grow so heavy that moving air can no longer hold them up. Fog and mist do not count, because their vapour does not condense enough to fall.

paragraphs.heading: From vapour to drops
paragraphs.text: Before anything can fall, the air must become saturated, which happens by cooling it, by adding water vapour, or both. The dew point is the temperature to which air must be cooled for this to happen and for vapour to turn to water. Vapour usually condenses first on particles called condensation nuclei, such as dust, ice and salt, and so forms clouds. Inside the cloud, small droplets merge by bumping into other drops or ice crystals until they are big enough to fall.

paragraphs.heading: How it is produced
paragraphs.text: The processes that produce precipitation include convective, stratiform and orographic ones. Convection involves strong up-and-down motions that can overturn the air in one spot within an hour and bring heavy downpours, while stratiform processes have gentler rising air and lighter precipitation. Short, intense bursts of rain in scattered places are called showers. In mountains, heavy falls are possible on windward slopes where air is pushed upward, while the far side can be desert, dried out because the air there is heated by compression. Most of the world's precipitation falls in the tropics and comes from convection.

paragraphs.heading: Liquid, freezing and frozen
paragraphs.text: Precipitation falls into three groups: liquid, liquid that freezes when it touches the surface, and ice. Rain and drizzle are the liquid kinds. When they freeze on contact within air below freezing, they are called freezing rain or freezing drizzle. The frozen kinds include snow, ice needles, ice pellets, hail and graupel, and several types can fall at the same time.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring it
paragraphs.text: Rain is usually caught in a rain gauge and reported as a depth in millimetres. A millimetre of rain is the same as one litre of water landing on each square metre. Snow is caught in a snow gauge or container and measured as a height in centimetres, and it can be melted to give a water equivalent in millimetres. Because snow holds differing amounts of water, that figure gives only a rough idea of snow depth.

paragraphs.heading: Earth's fresh water supply
paragraphs.text: Precipitation is a major part of the water cycle and delivers most of the planet's fresh water. Every year about 505,000 cubic kilometres of water falls, 398,000 over the oceans and 107,000 over land. Spread over the globe, that is an average of 990 millimetres a year, but only 715 millimetres over land. Climate systems such as the Köppen classification use yearly rainfall to tell climates apart, and global warming is already raising precipitation in some regions and lowering it in others. It even happens beyond Earth: on Titan, Saturn's largest moon, methane falls as a slow drizzle.
